decisions.title: Tasks and Worktree Lanes Are Different Layers
decisions.description: Tasks describe the goal (what to do). Worktrees describe where execution happens (isolated directory). Keeping these layers separate prevents the runtime model from blurring: a task can exist without a worktree, and a worktree can exist without an active task. The binding between them is explicit and optional.
decisions.alternatives: Folding worktree state into task records conflates goal and location. Requiring every task to have a worktree adds overhead for trivial tasks. Separate records with optional binding is the cleanest model.

decisions.title: Explicit enter / run / closeout Lifecycle
decisions.description: Worktree operations follow a defined lifecycle: allocate the worktree, enter the directory, run the work, then decide whether to keep or remove it during closeout. Each step is a separate tool operation, making the lifecycle inspectable and recoverable. Partial failures (crash during execution) leave the worktree in a known state.
decisions.alternatives: Auto-managing worktrees invisibly makes failures mysterious. Combining all lifecycle steps into one operation reduces flexibility and prevents partial recovery.

decisions.title: Lifecycle Events Make Lanes Observable
decisions.description: Create, enter, and closeout events are emitted to an append-only event stream (.worktrees/events.jsonl). This makes execution-lane state visible to the rest of the system without querying each worktree individually. Events are the side channel for observability; task and worktree files remain the source of truth.
decisions.alternatives: Querying each worktree's git status is slow and doesn't capture transitions. Console logs are ephemeral and hard to audit. A full event bus is powerful but heavier than needed.
